title: What is Bioluminescence?
description:
The season is called BIOGLOW — so let's learn about how nature actually glows! **Bioluminescence** is when living things produce their own light through a chemical reaction inside their bodies.

**How it works:**
A molecule called **luciferin** reacts with oxygen, helped by an enzyme called **luciferase**. The reaction releases energy as light — a cold light, with almost no heat. (A light bulb wastes most of its energy as heat; a firefly wastes almost none!)

**Who glows?**
- **Fireflies** — flash patterns to find mates
- **Anglerfish** — dangle a glowing lure to attract prey in the deep sea
- **Dinoflagellates (glowing plankton)** — light up waves and footprints on beaches when disturbed
- **Glowing fungi** — like the ghost fungus, glow to attract insects that spread their spores
- **Vampire squid & jellyfish** — flash or squirt glowing mucus to confuse predators

**Why glow?** The big four reasons: finding mates, attracting prey, scaring or confusing predators, and communication.

title: Ecosystems Where Things Glow
description:
Bioluminescence shows up in some of Earth's most amazing — and most threatened — ecosystems. Understanding WHERE things glow helps you understand WHY those ecosystems matter.

**The deep sea** — Below 1,000 meters, sunlight never reaches. It's the largest habitat on Earth, and over 75% of deep-sea animals make their own light! Threats: deep-sea mining, trawling, warming oceans.

**Bioluminescent bays** — A few rare bays (like Mosquito Bay in Puerto Rico) are so full of glowing plankton that the water lights up at night. Threats: water pollution, boat traffic, coastal development that dims the glow.

**Forests at night** — Fireflies need dark nights, moist soil, and undisturbed leaf litter. Threats: light pollution (artificial light confuses their flash signals!), pesticides, habitat loss. Firefly populations are declining worldwide.

**Caves and fungi zones** — Glow-worms in caves and glowing fungi on rotting logs depend on stable, untouched habitats.

**The big idea:** when an ecosystem gets polluted, developed, or lit up at night, the glow is often the first thing to disappear. Bioluminescence is like a health meter for these ecosystems.

**What is an ecosystem?**
An ecosystem is a community of living things (plants, animals, fungi, bacteria) interacting with each other and their environment. Healthy ecosystems provide clean air, water, food, and stability for all life on Earth.

**What is biodiversity?**
Biodiversity means the variety of life in an area. The more diverse an ecosystem, the more resilient it is — like a team where everyone has different skills.

**What is nature-inspired technology (biomimicry)?**
Biomimicry is when engineers look to nature for design ideas. Examples: Velcro was inspired by burrs, bullet trains shaped like kingfisher beaks, solar panels modeled on leaves.

title: Hub Check: Find a Reliable Gyro
description:
Not all SPIKE hubs are equal! Some hubs have gyro sensors that **drift** — the angle reading slowly changes even when the hub is sitting perfectly still. A drifting gyro will ruin your turns and straight-line driving all season.

**Your mission:** Test at least 2 hubs and find the most reliable one for your team.

**How to test for drift:**
1. Place the hub flat on the table and don't touch it
2. Run the test code below and watch the angle reading for 60 seconds
3. A good gyro stays at 0 (or flickers ±1 at most). A bad gyro slowly climbs: 0... 1... 2... 3...

**How to test responsiveness:**
1. Run the code, then rotate the hub exactly 90° using a corner of the table as a guide
2. A good gyro reads 89–91. A bad one is off by 3° or more.
codeExample:
from pybricks.hubs import PrimeHub
from pybricks.tools import wait, StopWatch

hub = PrimeHub()
hub.imu.reset_heading(0)

timer = StopWatch()

# Watch the heading for 60 seconds while the hub sits still.
# A good gyro stays at 0. A bad one drifts: 1, 2, 3...
while timer.time() < 60000:
    print("Heading:", hub.imu.heading())
    wait(1000)

title: Motor Check: Find a Matched Pair
description:
Your drive motors are the legs of your robot. If the left motor spins even slightly faster than the right, your robot will curve when it should drive straight — and no amount of code can fully fix a bad motor pair.

**Your mission:** Test your motors and find the best-matched pair for your drive base.

**What makes a good pair:**
1. **Same speed** — when both are set to the same power, they should report nearly identical speeds
2. **Low friction** — spin each motor shaft gently by hand with no program running. It should turn smoothly with no gritty or stiff spots

**How to test:** Connect two motors to ports A and B, run the code below, and record the reported speeds. Swap motors between tests so every motor gets tested.
codeExample:
from pybricks.hubs import PrimeHub
from pybricks.pupdevices import Motor
from pybricks.parameters import Port
from pybricks.tools import wait

hub = PrimeHub()
motor_a = Motor(Port.A)
motor_b = Motor(Port.B)

# Run both motors at the same command for 3 seconds,
# then print actual measured speed of each.
motor_a.run(500)   # 500 deg/s
motor_b.run(500)
wait(3000)

print("Motor A speed:", motor_a.speed())
print("Motor B speed:", motor_b.speed())

motor_a.stop()
motor_b.stop()

title: What is Bioluminescence?
description:
The season is called BIOGLOW — so let's learn about how nature actually glows! **Bioluminescence** is when living things produce their own light through a chemical reaction inside their bodies.

**How it works:**
A molecule called **luciferin** reacts with oxygen, helped by an enzyme called **luciferase**. The reaction releases energy as light — a cold light, with almost no heat. (A light bulb wastes most of its energy as heat; a firefly wastes almost none!)

**Who glows?**
- **Fireflies** — flash patterns to find mates
- **Anglerfish** — dangle a glowing lure to attract prey in the deep sea
- **Dinoflagellates (glowing plankton)** — light up waves and footprints on beaches when disturbed
- **Glowing fungi** — like the ghost fungus, glow to attract insects that spread their spores
- **Vampire squid & jellyfish** — flash or squirt glowing mucus to confuse predators

**Why glow?** The big four reasons: finding mates, attracting prey, scaring or confusing predators, and communication.

title: Ecosystems Where Things Glow
description:
Bioluminescence shows up in some of Earth's most amazing — and most threatened — ecosystems. Understanding WHERE things glow helps you understand WHY those ecosystems matter.

**The deep sea** — Below 1,000 meters, sunlight never reaches. It's the largest habitat on Earth, and over 75% of deep-sea animals make their own light! Threats: deep-sea mining, trawling, warming oceans.

**Bioluminescent bays** — A few rare bays (like Mosquito Bay in Puerto Rico) are so full of glowing plankton that the water lights up at night. Threats: water pollution, boat traffic, coastal development that dims the glow.

**Forests at night** — Fireflies need dark nights, moist soil, and undisturbed leaf litter. Threats: light pollution (artificial light confuses their flash signals!), pesticides, habitat loss. Firefly populations are declining worldwide.

**Caves and fungi zones** — Glow-worms in caves and glowing fungi on rotting logs depend on stable, untouched habitats.

**The big idea:** when an ecosystem gets polluted, developed, or lit up at night, the glow is often the first thing to disappear. Bioluminescence is like a health meter for these ecosystems.

title: Hub Check: Find a Reliable Gyro
description:
Not all SPIKE hubs are equal! Some hubs have gyro sensors that **drift** — the angle reading slowly changes even when the hub is sitting perfectly still. A drifting gyro will ruin your turns and straight-line driving all season.

**Your mission:** Test at least 2 hubs and find the most reliable one for your team.

**How to test for drift:**
1. Place the hub flat on the table and don't touch it
2. Run the test code below and watch the angle reading for 60 seconds
3. A good gyro stays at 0 (or flickers ±1 at most). A bad gyro slowly climbs: 0... 1... 2... 3...

**How to test responsiveness:**
1. Run the code, then rotate the hub exactly 90° using a corner of the table as a guide
2. A good gyro reads 89–91. A bad one is off by 3° or more.
codeExample:
from pybricks.hubs import PrimeHub
from pybricks.tools import wait, StopWatch

hub = PrimeHub()
hub.imu.reset_heading(0)

timer = StopWatch()

# Watch the heading for 60 seconds while the hub sits still.
# A good gyro stays at 0. A bad one drifts: 1, 2, 3...
while timer.time() < 60000:
    print("Heading:", hub.imu.heading())
    wait(1000)

description:
Your drive motors are the legs of your robot. If the left motor spins even slightly faster than the right, your robot will curve when it should drive straight — and no amount of code can fully fix a bad motor pair.

**Your mission:** Test your motors and find the best-matched pair for your drive base.

**What makes a good pair:**
1. **Same speed** — when both are set to the same power, they should report nearly identical speeds
2. **Low friction** — spin each motor shaft gently by hand with no program running. It should turn smoothly with no gritty or stiff spots

**How to test:** Connect two motors to ports A and B, run the code below, and record the reported speeds. Swap motors between tests so every motor gets tested.
codeExample:
from pybricks.hubs import PrimeHub
from pybricks.pupdevices import Motor
from pybricks.parameters import Port
from pybricks.tools import wait

hub = PrimeHub()
motor_a = Motor(Port.A)
motor_b = Motor(Port.B)

# Run both motors at the same command for 3 seconds,
# then print actual measured speed of each.
motor_a.run(500)   # 500 deg/s
motor_b.run(500)
wait(3000)

print("Motor A speed:", motor_a.speed())
print("Motor B speed:", motor_b.speed())

motor_a.stop()
motor_b.stop()

title: Step 2 — Pick Your Problem
description:
Every great Innovation Project starts with a clearly defined problem. Not "pollution is bad" — that's too big. A great FLL problem is **specific, real, and affects real people or ecosystems**.

**A strong problem statement answers:**
1. **WHO** is affected? (people, animals, an ecosystem)
2. **WHAT** exactly is the problem?
3. **WHERE** does it happen? (bonus points if it's local!)
4. **WHY** does it matter?

**Example:** "Fireflies in our county are disappearing because streetlights and porch lights confuse their mating flashes. Local kids may grow up never seeing a firefly." — specific, local, and you can picture who loses.

Use everything you learned in your research assignments (bioluminescence, glowing ecosystems, expert research) to pick the problem your team will solve this season.

description:
Judges ALWAYS ask: **"How is your solution different from what already exists?"** Teams that can't answer lose points. Teams that can answer confidently stand out.

Your mission: find out what's already being done about your problem. For each existing solution, figure out what it does well and where it falls short — that gap is where YOUR innovation lives.

**Where to look:**
- Search "[your problem] solution" and "[your problem] technology"
- Check what organizations and companies are doing
- Ask the experts you identified in your research
- Look at how OTHER countries handle the same problem

title: Step 7 — Share, Get Feedback & Improve
description:
FLL judges give top Innovation scores to teams who **shared their solution with real people and improved it based on feedback**. This is the step most teams skip — don't be most teams!

**Who to share with:**
- An expert from your research list (email works!)
- A teacher, parent, or community member connected to the problem
- Another FLL team or your classmates

**What to ask them:**
1. "Does this solution make sense to you?"
2. "What problems do you see with it?"
3. "What would make it better?"

Then — and this is the important part — **actually change something** based on what they said, and document what you changed.

title: Step 9 — Write Your Presentation Script 🎬
description:
Deliverable #1 of 3! Your Innovation Project presentation is **5 minutes max** in front of the judges. A written script keeps you on time, makes sure nothing gets forgotten, and gives every teammate a speaking part.

**The winning 5-part structure:**
1. **The Hook (30 sec)** — grab attention! A surprising fact, a question, a mini skit
2. **The Problem (1 min)** — who, what, where, why — with your evidence
3. **Existing Solutions & The Gap (1 min)** — what's out there, and what's missing
4. **Your Solution (1.5 min)** — name it, explain it, show how it fills the gap
5. **Sharing & Impact (1 min)** — who you shared with, what you improved, what's next

**Pro tips:** every teammate speaks · practice with a timer · the hook is what judges remember — make it fun!

Deliverable #2 of 3! Slides support your script — they don't replace it. Judges should watch YOU, not read a wall of text.

**The 6-slide formula (one per script part, plus a title):**
1. **Title slide** — team name, solution name, a great image
2. **Hook slide** — one striking image or one big number
3. **Problem slide** — a photo + 3 bullet points max
4. **Existing solutions slide** — your comparison in simple visual form
5. **Solution slide** — your sketch/diagram front and center
6. **Impact slide** — who you shared with + what you changed

**Slide rules that win:**
- Max 6 words per bullet, max 3 bullets per slide
- Big images beat small text
- One idea per slide
- Practice clicking through while speaking — slides should match your script's flow

title: Step 13 — Memorize Your Script & Full Rehearsal 🎤

Competition-ready means **no reading from paper**. Judges connect with teams who speak to them, not at a script. Time to memorize and rehearse until your presentation is smooth.

**The memorization ladder:**
1. Read your part out loud 5 times

- Under 5 minutes every time

- You can answer: 'What was the hardest part?' and 'What would you do next?' — judges always ask follow-ups!

Great teams never run with their FIRST idea — they brainstorm MANY ideas and pick the best. Today there are no bad ideas: quantity beats quality, wild ideas welcome, build on each other.

title: Step 4 — Choose Your Solution & Plan Your Iterations 🗺️
description:
You have a problem (Step 2), you know the gap (Step 3), and you have a pile of solution ideas (Step 1). Now: **choose your solution and plan how it will evolve**.

Real engineers never design something once — they iterate. Plan your iterations BEFORE you start so every version has a purpose:

- **Iteration 1 (v1)** — the first rough draft. Goal: get the idea on paper
- **Iteration 2 (v2)** — the improvement pass. Goal: fix what the team finds weak in v1
- **Iteration 3 (final)** — the feedback pass. Goal: improve based on what real people tell you

For each iteration, decide: what is the GOAL of this version? What will you test or question? What does success look like?

Now that you have a topic, become a curious detective! Great researchers start with **questions**, not answers. The better your questions, the better your project.

- **Who** is affected? (People? Animals? A whole ecosystem?)
- **Why** is it happening? (What are the causes?)

- Write EVERY idea down, even the goofy ones

photoPrompt: Upload DRAWINGS or sketches of your solution — hand-drawn is perfect! Add as many as you need.
description:
Time to pick ONE solution and make it your team's own. Judges reward solutions that are **unique** — different from what already exists, or a real improvement on it.

**Make your solution unique:**
1. Pick your best idea from the brainstorm
2. Search: does something like this already exist? (Add the links you find below.)
3. Add your OWN twist — what makes yours different or better?

**Show it with drawings:** you do not need to build anything yet. **Draw** your solution — what it looks like, how it works, who uses it. Upload photos of your sketches. A labeled drawing tells judges more than a paragraph!

**Share your research links** so your coach can see what already exists and how yours is different.

title: Innovation Basics 5 — Build a LEGO Prototype
photoPrompt: Upload photos of your LEGO prototype from at least 2 angles. Close-ups of key parts are great too!
description:
Make your idea REAL with LEGO! A prototype is a first model of your solution — it does NOT have to work or be perfect. LEGO is a fast, fun way to show what your idea looks like and how the parts fit together.

**How to build a LEGO prototype:**
1. Look at your drawings from the last assignment
2. Use LEGO bricks, Technic beams, gears, or minifigures to represent the parts of your solution
3. Build FAST — aim to finish in one session, not to make it beautiful
4. **Photograph it from at least 2 angles** and upload the photos
5. Label the parts: what does each LEGO piece represent in the real solution?

**Tip:** if a part of your solution is not a physical object (like an app or a rule), build a LEGO model of the PLACE or PEOPLE it affects, and show how your solution helps.

title: Innovation Basics 6 — Model It in Tinkercad (3D)
photoPrompt: Upload a SCREENSHOT of your Tinkercad design. Take it right from your Tinkercad screen.
description:
Level up your prototype with **Tinkercad** — a free online 3D design tool. Turning your idea into a 3D model makes it look real and professional, and it is a skill judges love to see.

**Getting started with Tinkercad:**
1. Go to **tinkercad.com** and sign in (your coach can share a class code)
2. Click **Create → 3D Design**
3. Drag shapes onto the workplane to build your solution
4. Resize, rotate, and combine shapes to match your LEGO prototype
5. Add a **Hole** shape and group it to cut out openings

**Your mission:** recreate or improve your prototype as a 3D Tinkercad model. Then **modify it** — change at least one thing to make it better than your LEGO version.

**When you finish:** click **Share → Invite people / Copy link**, paste the link below, and upload a screenshot of your design.

title: Robot Build Photo Log
photoPrompt: Snap a photo of your robot at the END of today’s build session. Add a new photo each session to build your log!
description:
Judges LOVE to see how your robot grew over time. This is your **build photo log** — take a picture of your robot at the end of every build session so you have a visual story from empty baseplate to competition machine.

**Why this matters:**
- Shows judges your engineering PROCESS, not just the finished robot
- Helps your team remember what you changed and why
- Makes your engineering notebook look amazing

**Each session:**
1. Build or improve your robot
2. **Photograph it** from the front and side before you pack up
3. Write one line about what you added or fixed today

title: Wiring Map: Photograph Your Ports
photoPrompt: Upload a clear, close-up photo of your hub showing which motors and sensors are plugged into which ports.
description:
When an attachment breaks at competition or a program acts weird, the first thing to check is: **is everything plugged into the right port?** A wiring photo saves you every time.

**Your mission:** take a close-up photo of your SPIKE hub showing every cable, then map out what is plugged into each port. This is exactly what your code's `Motor(Port.B)` lines have to match!

**Tip:** label your cables with tape (B, C, D, F...) so a photo instantly shows the setup.

Do the ports in your photo match the Port letters in your code? Double-check!

title: Robot Glamour Shots: Competition Photos
photoPrompt: Upload clean, well-lit photos of your FINAL robot from the front, side, top, and a close-up of your favorite attachment.
description:
Your robot is competition-ready — now show it off! These **glamour shots** go in your engineering notebook and your Robot Design judging slides.

**How to take great robot photos:**
- Use good lighting (near a window works great)
- Put the robot on a clean, plain surface
- Take photos from **4 angles**: front, side, top, and a close-up of a cool attachment
- Hold the camera steady — no blur!

**Then describe your design choices** so judges understand WHY your robot looks the way it does.
